qs.q: An experimental drug prolongs the open state of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. What is the primary electrophysiological result recorded in the muscle fiber?
o: A prolonged end‑plate potential that keeps the muscle fiber depolarized.
A brief hyperpolarization caused by excessive potassium efflux.
An immediate block of all action potentials due to sodium channel closure.
A series of high‑frequency rhythmic oscillations in resting membrane tension.
An irreversible shift of the resting membrane potential toward more negative values.
qs.e: Prolonged channel opening allows continuous inward sodium current, sustaining an endplate potential that keeps the muscle membrane depolarized.

qs.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis has antibodies against acetylcholine receptors. What is the primary effect on the neuromuscular junction?
o: Increased frequency of miniature end-plate potentials at the motor end plate
Decreased release of acetylcholine from the presynaptic nerve terminal
Increased sensitivity of the muscle fiber to acetylcholine binding
Reduced depolarization of opioid muscle fiber membrane at the end plate
Enhanced reuptake of acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft
qs.e: Antibodies block or destroy acetylcholine receptors, reducing the number of functional receptors and thus the depolarization of the muscle fiber.

qs.q: In a study on cardiac pacemaking cells, acetylcholine is applied to the preparation. Which cellular mechanism accounts for the resulting decrease in heart rate?
o: Stimulation of L-type calcium channel currents
Inhibition of funny current channel preparations
Activation of G-protein coupled potassium channels
Enhancement of sarcoplasmic calcium uptake rates
qs.e: Acetylcholine binds M2 receptors, activating G-protein coupled K+ channels that hyperpolarize pacemaker cells and slow firing.

qs.q: A pharmacological agent is administered to study junctional transmission. The drug competitively blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. What is the immediate physiological outcome?
o: Voltage-gated calcium channels in the motor axon terminal close
Acetylcholine accumulates in the synaptic cleft and causes tetany
End-plate potentials fail to reach threshold, preventing muscle contraction
Acetylcholinesterase activity increases, breaking down transmitter faster
Sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium spontaneously without stimulus
qs.e: Blocking nicotinic receptors prevents acetylcholine from generating a large enough end-plate potential to reach threshold.

qs.q: Which medication is used to treat the glandular manifestations of Sjogren’s Syndrome by increasing acetylcholine?
qs.e: The note lists parasympathomimetics like pilocarpine and cevimeline as treatments that increase acetylcholine to stimulate saliva production. Immunosuppressants are for extraglandular manifestations.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens with exertion. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are detected. What is the frequency of associated thymic abnormalities in this condition?
o: Thymic hyperplasia in about 30% and thymoma in 10%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 80% and thymoma in 50%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 10% and thymoma in 30%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 50% and thymoma in 80%
qs.e: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymic hyperplasia in about 30 percent of patients (especially younger ones) and thymoma in about 10 percent. Thymic abnormalities are not universal or entirely absent as implied by the incorrect options.

qs.q: A patient presents with high gastric acid production stimulated via the vagus nerve. Which specific receptor does acetylcholine bind to on parietal cells to achieve this?
qs.e: Acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve binds to M3 muscarinic receptors to increase intracellular calcium and activate the proton pump. H2 receptors are instead activated by histamine.

qs.q: Which cellular receptors are transmembrane proteins that open a central pore in response to a chemical messenger like acetylcholine?
qs.e: Ion channel receptors open or close a central pore upon ligand binding to allow ion flow. GPCRs and kinase-linked receptors operate via different enzymatic and second-messenger cascades.

ai.title: Acetylcholine Physiology and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Acetylcholine is a crucial neurotransmitter involved in neuromuscular transmission, autonomic function, and cognition. It acts on both nicotinic (ion channel) and muscarinic (G-protein coupled) receptors. Imbalances or disruptions in acetylcholine signaling can lead to significant clinical conditions.

sections.p: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a primary neurotransmitter in the peripheral and central nervous systems. It is synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA by the enzyme choline acetyltransferase and broken down by acetylcholinesterase. Its diverse roles make it vital for many bodily functions.
b: Primary neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system (both preganglionic and postganglionic synapses).
Neurotransmitter at sympathetic preganglionic synapses.
Essential for neuromuscular transmission at the skeletal muscle motor end plate.
Plays a significant role in memory, attention, and other cognitive functions in the central nervous system.

sections.p: Acetylcholine exerts its effects by binding to two main types of receptors: nicotinic and muscarinic. The type of receptor determines the cellular response, which can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the specific receptor subtype and tissue.
b: Nicotinic receptors: Ligand-gated ion channels found at the neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia, and in the central nervous system. Binding of ACh causes rapid depolarization.

Muscarinic receptors: G-protein coupled receptors found in the central nervous system and on effector organs of the parasympathetic nervous system (e.g., heart, smooth muscle, glands). Their effects are slower and can be excitatory or inhibitory.
At the neuromuscular junction, ACh released from motor nerve terminals binds to nicotinic receptors on muscle fibers, initiating muscle contraction.
In the autonomic nervous system, ACh mediates communication between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons, and between postganglionic parasympathetic neurons and their target organs.

sections.p: The precise regulation of acetylcholine synthesis, release, and degradation is critical for normal physiological function. Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) rapidly breaks down ACh in the synaptic cleft, ensuring transient signaling and allowing for precise control of neuronal and muscular activity.
b: Synthesis: Choline acetyltransferase combines choline and acetyl-CoA.
Release: Calcium-dependent exocytosis from presynaptic terminals.
Degradation: Acetylcholinesterase hydrolyzes ACh into choline and acetate, terminating its action.
Reuptake: Choline is transported back into the presynaptic neuron for recycling.

sections.p: Dysregulation of acetylcholine signaling is implicated in several neurological and neuromuscular disorders. Both excess and deficiency of ACh can lead to significant clinical manifestations, affecting motor control, autonomic function, and cognition.
b: Myasthenia Gravis: Auto-antibodies target and destroy nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, leading to fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest.

Alzheimer's Disease: Characterized by significant loss of cholinergic neurons in the brain, contributing to cognitive decline, memory loss, and attention deficits. Amyloid-β deposition and tau tangles are also key features.
Delirium: Often associated with an imbalance of neurotransmitters, including acetylcholine deficiency and relative dopaminergic excess, leading to acute confusion and altered consciousness.
Parkinson's Disease: While primarily a dopamine deficiency, there is a relative excess of acetylcholine due to the dopamine loss, contributing to rigidity and tremor.

Organophosphate Poisoning: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase leads to excessive accumulation of ACh, causing overstimulation of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors (cholinergic crisis).

sections.p: Understanding acetylcholine's role is crucial for diagnosing and managing various conditions. Pharmacological interventions often target acetylcholine synthesis, release, degradation, or its receptors to restore balance.
b: Bronchial smooth muscle: Innervated by parasympathetic nerves releasing ACh, causing bronchoconstriction. This pathway is targeted by bronchodilators in conditions like asthma.
Pupillary constriction: Mediated by muscarinic receptors in the iris sphincter muscle, a target for drugs like pilocarpine.
Heart rate: Parasympathetic stimulation via ACh slows heart rate by acting on muscarinic receptors in the SA and AV nodes.
Gastrointestinal motility: ACh increases gut motility and secretions via muscarinic receptors.
Anticholinergic drugs: Block ACh receptors, used to treat conditions like overactive bladder, motion sickness, and Parkinson's disease (to reduce tremor and rigidity).

t.b: Distinguishes myasthenia gravis from cholinergic crisis. Improvement in muscle strength after administration suggests myasthenia gravis; worsening suggests cholinergic crisis.

Confirms diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Presence of these auto-antibodies is highly specific for the condition. If unavailable, clinical suspicion and response to anticholinesterase inhibitors guide management.

Evaluates for amyloid-β and tau protein levels in suspected Alzheimer's disease. Reduced amyloid-β and increased tau support the diagnosis. Often unavailable in low-resource settings, so clinical assessment and cognitive tests are paramount.

sections.p: When considering acetylcholine, think about its diverse roles across different systems and how disruptions manifest clinically. Focus on the receptor types and the consequences of their activation or blockade.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe muscle weakness, especially affecting breathing or swallowing
Acute confusion or altered mental status
Excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, or muscle twitching

faq.q: What is the difference between nicotinic and muscarinic receptors?
faq.a: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels that cause rapid depolarization, found at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia. Muscarinic receptors are G-protein coupled receptors with slower, more varied effects, found on parasympathetic target organs and in the brain.

faq.q: Why is acetylcholine important for memory?
faq.a: Acetylcholine plays a crucial role in learning, memory, and attention in the brain. Loss of cholinergic neurons is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, contributing to cognitive decline.

Choline, a precursor to acetylcholine, is an essential nutrient found in foods like eggs, meat, and legumes. Adequate dietary choline is necessary for acetylcholine synthesis, though severe deficiencies are rare.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic exam to identify acetylcholine‑related neuromuscular dysfunction, autonomic imbalance or cholinergic toxicity.
b: Ask about fluctuating muscle weakness, ptosis, diplopia, fatigue worsening with activity, and respiratory difficulty.
Inquire about dry mouth, dry eyes, constipation, urinary urgency, sweating, bradycardia, and bronchospasm.
Check for exposure to organophosphates, pesticides, or nerve agents.
Ask about recent infections, thymic surgery, or autoimmune disease history.
Review medications that inhibit acetylcholinesterase or block nicotinic receptors.
Examine cranial nerves for ptosis, extraocular movement restriction, and facial weakness.
Test for fatigable weakness by repeated finger‑to‑thumb or sustained isometric contraction.
Assess autonomic function: heart rate variability, blood pressure response to standing, pupil size and reactivity.
Perform a bedside edrophonium test if MG is suspected (observe rapid improvement).
Check for signs of cholinergic crisis: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, emesis, and muscle fasciculations.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use laboratory, electrophysiological and imaging tests to confirm diagnosis, gauge severity and guide therapy.

t.b: Positive >0.4 nmol/L confirms MG; higher titres correlate with generalized disease.
Jitter >50 µs or blocking >10% is highly sensitive for MG; normal in healthy controls.
Low‑frequency RNS shows decremental response; high‑frequency may reveal incremental response in Lambert‑Eaton.
Level <2000 U/L suggests organophosphate exposure; normal values >3000 U/L.
Low activity indicates susceptibility to succinylcholine or organophosphate poisoning.
Detect thymic hyperplasia or thymoma; essential for surgical planning.
Reduced vital capacity or maximal inspiratory pressure indicates respiratory involvement.

t.a: Serum electrolytes, renal and liver function
t.b: Abnormalities can mimic or worsen cholinergic symptoms; correct before therapy.
Confirm exposure when clinical suspicion is high.

sections.p: Apply established criteria to classify disease and plan treatment.
b: Generalised MG: anti‑AChR antibodies positive or SFEMG abnormal; ocular MG: antibodies negative, ocular symptoms only.
Severity grading (MGFA): I (ocular) to V (intubation required).
Thymic status: normal, hyperplasia, or thymoma – influences surgical decision.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor responsiveness: improvement after pyridostigmine indicates functional receptors.
Organophosphate poisoning: clinical triad plus low cholinesterase confirms diagnosis.

sections.p: Differentiate from other neuromuscular or autonomic disorders.

t.b: Autonomic symptoms, proximal weakness, incremental response on high‑frequency RNS; antibodies against P/Q‑type Ca²⁺ channels.
Descending paralysis, cranial nerve involvement, preserved reflexes, no fatigability; toxin blocks ACh release.
Proximal weakness, elevated CK, no fatigability, normal EMG.
Sensory loss, distal weakness, absent reflexes, nerve conduction studies abnormal.

sections.p: A structured approach helps treat disorders of acetylcholine transmission such as myasthenia gravis, organophosphate poisoning and cholinergic crisis.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation – give high‑flow O₂ and secure airway if respiratory muscles are weak.
2. Identify the underlying aetiology (autoimmune, toxic, drug‑induced) with history, exam and targeted tests.
3. Initiate symptomatic therapy: anticholinesterase (e.g., pyridostigmine) for myasthenia gravis; atropine for cholinergic excess; pralidoxime for organophosphate poisoning.

4. Start disease‑modifying treatment where appropriate: immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate) or thymectomy for generalized myasthenia gravis; decontamination and supportive care for poisoning.
5. Monitor neuromuscular strength (e.g., quantitative MG score), pupil size, heart rate and secretions; repeat labs (acetylcholinesterase activity, antibody titres) as indicated.
6. Escalate to intensive care if vital capacity falls below 15 mL/kg, if there is worsening bradycardia, or if refractory cholinergic crisis persists despite anticholinergic therapy.
7. Refer for specialist input (neurology, toxicology) when diagnosis is uncertain, when thymic imaging shows mass, or when resources for plasma exchange are needed.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse effects and interactions of cholinergic and anticholinergic agents prevents iatrogenic complications.
b: Anticholinesterases may cause muscarinic excess: bradycardia, bronchospasm, diarrhoea, increased salivation – treat with atropine if severe.
Excessive nicotinic blockade (e.g., curare‑type agents) leads to muscle weakness and respiratory failure – provide ventilatory support and reverse with cholinesterase inhibitor if appropriate.
Atropine and other antimuscarinics can precipitate tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mouth – avoid in patients with glaucoma or prostatic obstruction.
Beta‑blockers potentiate bradycardia when combined with cholinergic drugs – monitor heart rate and consider dose reduction.
Quinidine and other class Ia anti‑arrhythmics increase acetylcholinesterase inhibitor toxicity – avoid co‑administration.
Herbal cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., galantamine‑containing extracts) may augment pyridostigmine effects – inquire about traditional medicines.
Renal or hepatic impairment reduces clearance of pyridostigmine and atropine – adjust frequency and watch for accumulation.

sections.p: Complications arise from both disease progression and therapy; early recognition triggers escalation.
b: Myasthenic crisis: rapid decline in muscle strength, bulbar weakness, respiratory compromise – move to ICU, start plasma exchange or IVIG, and increase anticholinesterase dose cautiously.
Cholinergic crisis: excessive salivation, diaphoresis, bradycardia, fasciculations – give atropine, reduce anticholinesterase dose, consider pralidoxime if toxin exposure suspected.
Thymoma‑related paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., pure red cell aplasia) – obtain CT chest, refer to thoracic surgery; treat underlying tumour.
Organophosphate poisoning delayed neuropathy – monitor for peripheral neuropathy weeks after exposure; provide physiotherapy and supportive care.
Long‑term anticholinesterase therapy may cause cholinergic side‑effects limiting dose – consider immunosuppression or thymectomy as definitive options.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions and environmental factors modify presentation, test results and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV infection can cause opportunistic neuropathies that mimic neuromuscular weakness; CD4 count guides need for prophylactic antibiotics.
Active tuberculosis may require rifampicin, which induces hepatic enzymes and lowers plasma levels of pyridostigmine – monitor clinical response.
Severe malnutrition reduces choline stores, potentially lowering acetylcholine synthesis; supplement dietary choline when possible.
Pregnancy increases plasma volume and renal clearance, possibly reducing anticholinesterase effectiveness – monitor strength more frequently.
Diabetes mellitus can cause autonomic neuropathy with baseline tachycardia; avoid high‑dose anticholinergics that may worsen orthostatic hypotension.
Alcohol use potentiates central depressant effects of cholinergic excess – counsel abstinence during crisis periods.
Renal failure prolongs atropine half‑life; use lower frequency and watch for anticholinergic toxicity.
Liver failure impairs metabolism of many anticholinesterases; dose adjustments and close monitoring are required.

sections.p: Tailoring management to vulnerable populations ensures safety and efficacy in low‑resource settings.
b: Children: use weight‑adjusted anticholinesterase dosing; avoid drugs with prolonged QT; monitor growth‑related changes in muscle strength.
Pregnancy: pyridostigmine is category B and generally safe; avoid high‑dose atropine unless life‑threatening cholinergic crisis.
Elderly: increased sensitivity to anticholinergic side‑effects; start with low‑dose anticholinesterase and titrate slowly.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections that can cause weakness; consider drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals.

Low‑resource settings: when acetylcholinesterase assays are unavailable, rely on clinical triad (SLUD) for organophosphate poisoning; use readily available atropine and pralidoxime kits; for myasthenia gravis, use bedside single‑fiber EMG if possible, otherwise base diagnosis on antibody titre (>0.4 nmol/L) and clinical pattern.

facts: Anti‑acetylcholine‑receptor antibody titre >0.4 nmol/L supports diagnosis of generalized myasthenia gravis.
Single‑fiber EMG jitter >50 µs (or blocking >10 %) is the most sensitive electrophysiologic marker for myasthenia gravis.
Serum cholinesterase <2000 U/L strongly suggests organophosphate poisoning in low‑resource settings.
Parietal cells express M₃ muscarinic receptors; ACh binding stimulates H⁺/K⁺‑ATPase and gastric acid secretion.
Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction are ligand‑gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels; blockade causes a rapid fall in end‑plate potential.
Muscarinic M₂ receptors dominate in the heart; ACh activation opens K⁺ channels, hyperpolarising SA node and slowing rate.
Pyridostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to improve neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis.
Organophosphate exposure is treated with atropine (muscarinic antagonist) plus pralidoxime (AChE reactivator).
In Sjögren’s syndrome, pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist) increases salivary and lacrimal secretion.
ACh synthesis requires choline acetyltransferase and acetyl‑CoA; deficiency of this enzyme is rare but causes congenital myasthenic syndrome.

mnemonics.t: Symptoms of ACh excess: Salivation, Abdominal cramps, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm – helps recall organophosphate toxicity.
M3 receptors mediate Muscarinic stimulation of gastric acid, smooth muscle contraction, and glandular secretion.

vivas.q: Define the primary physiological effect of anti‑acetylcholine‑receptor antibodies at the neuromuscular junction.
vivas.a: They reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors, decreasing end‑plate potentials and causing fatigable weakness.

vivas.q: Explain how acetylcholine decreases heart rate when applied to pacemaker cells.
vivas.a: ACh activates M₂ receptors, opening G‑protein‑gated K⁺ channels, hyperpolarising SA‑node cells and slowing diastolic depolarisation.

vivas.q: What immediate physiological change occurs after a competitive nicotinic blocker is given at the NMJ?
vivas.a: It prevents ACh from opening the nicotinic channel, causing a rapid fall in end‑plate potential and transient muscle weakness.

vivas.q: Which drug increases acetylcholine to treat glandular symptoms of Sjögren’s syndrome?
vivas.a: Pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, stimulates salivary and lacrimal secretion.

vivas.q: What proportion of myasthenia gravis patients have thymic abnormalities?
vivas.a: Approximately 70 % have thymic hyperplasia or thymoma; thymectomy is considered in many cases.

vivas.q: Identify the receptor subtype on parietal cells that mediates ACh‑induced acid secretion.
vivas.a: M₃ muscarinic receptors; binding triggers intracellular Ca²⁺ rise and activation of H⁺/K⁺‑ATPase.

vivas.q: Name the type of receptor that opens a central ion pore upon ACh binding.
State the false statement among typical ACh facts.
vivas.a: The false statement is that ACh primarily binds M₂ receptors on parietal cells; the correct receptor is M₃.

vivas.q: What bedside test assesses neuromuscular transmission in suspected myasthenia gravis?
vivas.a: Repeated‑stimulation EMG showing decremental response; single‑fiber EMG jitter >50 µs is more sensitive.

vivas.q: Why is atropine contraindicated in patients with severe bradycardia due to beta‑blocker overdose?
vivas.a: Atropine blocks vagal tone but does not address beta‑blockade; high‑dose glucagon is preferred.

vivas.q: In a patient with organophosphate poisoning, what is the role of pralidoxime?
vivas.a: It reactivates phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase if given before ‘aging’, restoring ACh breakdown.

vivas.q: List three confounding factors that may alter serum cholinesterase levels.
vivas.a: Liver disease, malnutrition, and chronic exposure to carbamate pesticides can lower levels.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line management of myasthenic crisis in a low‑resource hospital?
vivas.a: Plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin if available; otherwise high‑dose pyridostigmine and supportive ventilation.

vivas.q: How does pregnancy affect acetylcholinesterase activity and drug choice?
vivas.a: Physiologic increase in plasma cholinesterase may reduce efficacy of anticholinesterases; dose adjustment and monitoring are required.

vivas.q: Why must anticholinesterase drugs be avoided in patients with asthma?
vivas.a: Excess ACh can cause bronchoconstriction via muscarinic receptors, worsening airway obstruction.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a positive Tensilon test?
vivas.a: Transient improvement in muscle strength after edrophonium indicates functional ACh receptors, supporting myasthenia gravis.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old man with organophosphate exposure is given atropine. Which of the following best explains its effect?
o: It blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing bronchorrhea and bradycardia.
It inhibits nicotinic receptors at the NMJ.
It increases renal excretion of the toxin.
mcqs.e: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, relieving muscarinic signs of poisoning.

mcqs.q: Which drug would you prescribe to improve dry mouth in a patient with Sjögren’s syndrome?
mcqs.e: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that stimulates salivary secretion.

mcqs.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis is started on pyridostigmine. Which adverse effect is most likely?
mcqs.e: Reversible AChE inhibition increases GI motility, causing diarrhoea.

mcqs.q: During cardiac electrophysiology study, ACh is infused and heart rate falls. The primary ionic mechanism is:
o: Opening of K⁺ channels via M₂ receptors
mcqs.e: M₂ activation opens G‑protein‑gated K⁺ channels, hyperpolarising SA node.

mcqs.q: Which receptor subtype mediates ACh‑induced gastric acid secretion?
mcqs.e: Parietal cells express M₃ receptors that stimulate acid secretion.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with fluctuating ptosis is tested with edrophonium. She improves. Which statement is FALSE?
o: Edrophonium is a reversible AChE inhibitor.
The drug has a rapid onset of action.
mcqs.e: Improvement does not differentiate myasthenic from cholinergic crisis; both may respond.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to using neostigmine in a postoperative patient?
mcqs.e: Neostigmine increases muscarinic tone and can worsen bradycardia.

cases.v: A 27‑year‑old male farmer presents with sweating, salivation, miosis, and muscle fasciculations after spraying his field with an organophosphate pesticide. Pulse 58/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 94% on room air.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention?
qs.a: Administer atropine intravenously to antagonise muscarinic effects, followed by pralidoxime if available.

qs.q: If respiratory failure develops, what supportive measure is required?
qs.a: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation until neuromuscular function recovers.

mistakes: Confusing M₂ with M₃ receptors on parietal cells; the correct subtype for acid secretion is M₃.
Using >0.5 nmol/L as the positive cut‑off for anti‑AChR antibodies; the validated threshold is >0.4 nmol/L.
Stating single‑fiber EMG jitter >55 µs as abnormal; the accepted limit is >50 µs.
Assuming atropine alone reverses organophosphate toxicity; pralidoxime is required for AChE reactivation.
Prescribing anticholinesterases in uncontrolled asthma; excess ACh can precipitate bronchospasm.
Neglecting to consider thymic imaging in all myasthenia gravis patients; thymoma detection guides surgical decision.
